lines.text:
Order in the Court — How a Trial Works

A courtroom is a place where the law decides what is right and what is wrong. It is formal, serious, and carefully organised. Every person in the room has a specific role, and every word is recorded.

At the front, the judge sits behind the judge's bench — a raised desk that shows the authority of the court. A court seal on the wall behind displays the emblem of the justice system. The judge controls the trial, makes rulings on legal questions, and — if there is no jury — decides the verdict.

To the left sits the jury box, where twelve jury members listen to the evidence. They must decide if the accused person is guilty or not guilty. After hearing everything, they fill in a verdict form and announce their decision to the court.

Two tables face the judge. At the prosecution table, the prosecutor presents the case against the accused. At the defence table, the defence attorney argues that the accused is innocent. Both lawyers use a lectern when speaking to the jury.

The witness stand is near the judge's bench. A witness is a person who saw something important or has expert knowledge. Before speaking, the witness takes an oath — a promise to tell the truth — using an oath card. The prosecutor asks questions first. Then the defence attorney asks questions in a cross-examination. If a lawyer believes a question is unfair, they say 'Objection!' and the judge decides whether to allow it.

A bailiff keeps order in the courtroom and protects the judge. A court reporter types every word that is said — creating the official record of the trial. A clerk manages the court's documents, including the case file, evidence bags, and the witness list. An interpreter translates for anyone who does not speak the court's language.

A trial follows a clear process. First, a hearing determines whether there is enough evidence. A summons tells a person to appear in court. A subpoena forces a witness to come. The lawyers file motions and briefs — written legal arguments. After both sides present their testimony, the jury deliberates and delivers a verdict. If the accused is found guilty, the judge announces the sentence. If found not guilty, it is an acquittal. Either side may file an appeal to challenge the decision in a higher court.

Other legal documents include a warrant (permission to search or arrest), a complaint (the formal charge), an affidavit (a written statement made under oath), a contract, a deposition (recorded testimony outside the courtroom), and an injunction (a court order to stop someone from doing something).

The gallery — the seating area for the public — is separated from the court by a railing. Family members, journalists, and observers sit here. Handcuffs may be visible on a defendant who is considered dangerous. A badge identifies court officials.

The courtroom is where society draws its lines — between right and wrong, guilt and innocence, freedom and punishment. The language of law is precise for a reason: because in a courtroom, words have consequences.

lines.text: The UK has Magistrates' Courts (minor cases, no jury) and Crown Courts (serious cases, with jury). The Supreme Court is the highest court. Judges in Crown Court traditionally wear wigs and robes, though this is gradually changing.

lines.text: 'Lawyer' is the general term. In the UK: a 'solicitor' gives legal advice and prepares cases; a 'barrister' argues cases in court. In the US, 'attorney' is the common term for both roles. These distinctions are important for B2+ learners.

lines.text: A fundamental principle of English law: the defendant is presumed innocent until the prosecution proves guilt 'beyond reasonable doubt'. The burden of proof lies with the prosecution, not the defence.
lines.name: A fundamental principle of English law: the defendant is presumed innocent until the prosecution proves guilt 'beyond reasonable doubt'. The burden of proof lies with the prosecution, not the defence.

lines.text: Many legal phrases are used informally: 'case dismissed' (topic closed), 'I rest my case' (I've proved my point), 'objection!' (I disagree), 'no contest' (I won't argue). These come from American TV courtroom dramas.

lines.text: ✅ "The judge said the man was guilty of the crime."

lines.text: 'Guilty' is the adjective: 'He is guilty.' 'Guilt' is the noun: 'His guilt was clear.' 'Guilty of + crime': 'guilty of theft.' Don't mix up the noun and the adjective forms. Similarly: 'innocent' (adj) vs. 'innocence' (noun).

lines.text: 'Evidence' is uncountable — no 'a' and no plural. 'The police found evidence.' 'A piece of evidence.' 'The evidence shows that...' Not: 'an evidence' or 'evidences.' Similar: 'advice', 'information', 'research.'

lines.text: 'Accused of' — the preposition is always 'of.' 'She was accused of lying.' 'They accused him of fraud.' Related legal collocations: 'charged with' (a crime), 'convicted of' (a crime), 'sentenced to' (a punishment), 'guilty of' (a crime).

lines.text: 'Say' + that (no person needed): 'He said that he saw...' 'Tell' + person + that: 'He told the court that...' Never 'told that' without a person. 'She said she was innocent.' 'She told the judge she was innocent.'

lines.text: 'Last' (meaning 'continue for a period') is intransitive — no passive. 'The trial lasted three days' (past simple). 'The trial has lasted three days so far' (present perfect). Never 'has been lasted' — this verb doesn't take passive form in this meaning.
